extracted.intended_audience: newcomers/travellers (particularly European/English) to West Africa; colonial residents and administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Practical 19th-century advice for avoiding disease and surviving residence or travel on the West African coast, covering prevention (air, food, water, nets), remedies (quinine, calomel, arsenic, spirits) and parasite treatments (filariae, Guinea-worm).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding the danger of night air
rubrics_metrics.description: The best ways of avoiding the danger of the night air are--to have your evening meal about 6.30 or 7,--8 is too late; sleep under a mosquito curtain whether there are mosquitoes in your district or not, and have a meal before starting out in the morning, a good hot cup of tea or coffee and bread and butter...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific actionable items: eat an early evening meal (6:30–7:00), do not have dinner as late as 8; always sleep under a mosquito net/mosquito curtain even if no mosquitoes are visible; eat a morning meal (hot drink and bread) before setting out. These measures are presented as primary preventive actions against 'night air' fevers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of stimulants (alcohol) as prophylactic/supportive
rubrics_metrics.description: All the evidence is in favour of alcohol, of a proper sort, taken at proper times, and in proper quantities, being extremely valuable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples: missionaries (teetotal) pass medicals but have heavier mortality; Mr. Stanley: 'wine is the best form of stimulant, but that it should not be taken before the evening meal.' Beer has been associated with higher haematuric fever in parts of Cameroon. Advice is to use moderate, appropriate alcoholic stimulants (preferably wine, at proper times) rather than strict teetotalism; avoid beer in some districts as it may correlate with certain fevers. Author cautions that this requires scientific comparative observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boil drinking water thoroughly and store safely
rubrics_metrics.description: The safest way of dealing with water I know is to boil it hard for ten minutes at least, and then instantly pour it into a jar with a narrow neck, which plug up with a wad of fresh cotton-wool--not a cork;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step-by-step: (1) Boil water vigorously for at least ten minutes. (2) Immediately pour into a narrow-necked jar and plug with fresh cotton-wool (explicitly not a cork). (3) If you dislike flat boiled-water taste, plunge a bit of red-hot iron into it to improve taste. Filtering may be done before boiling, but filters do not reliably remove malarial microbes. Do not leave boiled or filtered water exposed (on verandah or in coolers) — exposure to night/day air can re-contaminate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely solely on filters, water-boys, or local assurances of purity
rubrics_metrics.description: One favourite haunt of mine gets its drinking water from a cemented hole... people of your intelligence trusting the trio of water, boys, and filter, in the way you do. ... a good filter is a very fine thing for clearing drinking water of hippopotami, crocodiles, water snakes, catfish... but if you think it is going to stop back the microbe of marsh fever--my good sir, you are mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipatterns: trusting that a filter, a boy, or local claims ensure safety. Filters remove large visible contaminants but will not reliably remove malarial microbes/other micro-organisms. Always boil after filtering; inspect sources (streams may be contaminated by washing, dead animals, cemeteries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Give up cold water (drinks) while on the Coast
rubrics_metrics.description: And remember that you must give up cold water, boiled or unboiled, altogether;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author advises avoiding cold drinks entirely (even boiled water when cold), implying cold beverages increase risk. Store and consume boiled water warm or at least not cold/exposed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quinine prophylaxis and dosing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember always your life hangs on quinine, and that it is most important to keep the system sensitive to it... by taking it when in a malarious district, say, in a dose of five grams a day, you keep down the malaria which you are bound... When you have got very chilled or over-tired, take an extra five grains with a little wine or spirit at any time...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use quinine prophylactically while resident in malarious districts (author gives 'say, in a dose of five grams a day' phrasing, and elsewhere refers to 'five grains' as an extra dose when chilled). To maintain effectiveness avoid constantly pouring heavy doses 'for nothing' (which may blunt sensitivity and cause side effects like deafness). If chilled/over-tired take an extra prophylactic dose (author: 'extra five grains' with wine/spirit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment protocol when fever appears and when no doctor is available
rubrics_metrics.description: When you know... that you are in for a fever, send for a doctor if you can. If, as generally happens, there is no doctor near to send for, take a compound calomel and colocynth pill, fifteen grains of quinine and a grain of opium, and go to bed wrapped up in the best blanket available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If physician unavailable: administer a compound calomel and colocynth pill plus 15 grains quinine and 1 grain opium, then go to bed wrapped in blankets; take lashings of hot tea or a hot lime-juice drink; in the hot stage avoid fanning and avoid cooling while perspiring; stay rolled in blankets until perspiring stage passes and remain in bed till next morning. After the attack continue quinine in five-grain doses up to 15–20 grains a day for a week, but omit the opium pill after initial treatment. (Author's advice reflects historical 19th-century remedies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overuse/misuse of quinine
rubrics_metrics.description: It is most important to keep the system sensitive to it, which you do not do if you keep on pouring in heavy doses of it for nothing and you make yourself deaf into the bargain. I have known people take sixty grains of quinine in a day...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not take large, unnecessary doses of quinine continuously; reserve heavy dosing for required treatment. Excessive habitual dosing can blunt prophylactic benefit and cause toxicity (e.g., deafness). Maintain appropriate prophylactic dosing rather than continual heavy dosing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of calomel and arsenic
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the new-comer remember, in dealing with quinine, calomel, arsenic, and spirits, that they are not castor sugar nor he a glass bottle, but let him use them all--the two first fairly frequently--not waiting for an attack of fever and then ladling them into himself with a spoon. The third, arsenic--a drug much thought of by the French... should not be taken except under a doctor's orders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calomel and (colocynth) are recommended to be used 'fairly frequently' (in author’s view) as part of preventive or early treatment; arsenic should only be used under medical supervision. Spirits are valuable for treating chills. Note: these are historical recommendations and the author cautions against unsupervised arsenic use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fever-stage behavioural guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Then, in the hot stage, don't go fanning about, nor in the perspiring stage, for if you get a chill then you may turn a mild dose of fever into a fatal one. If, however, you keep conscientiously rolled in your blanket until the perspiring stage is well over, and stay in bed till the next morning, the chances are you will be all right...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During fever: avoid fanning/cooling during the hot stage; remain wrapped in blankets through perspiration to avoid secondary chilling; stay in bed until the next morning. These behaviours are intended to prevent turning a mild fever into a fatal one by inducing chills during perspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain general health via exercise and good food to resist fever
rubrics_metrics.description: The great thing in West Africa is to keep up your health to a good level, that will enable you to resist fever, and it is exceedingly difficult for most people to do this, because of the difficulty of getting exercise and good food.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical focus on regular exercise and adequate nutritious food to raise baseline health and resistance to malarial/other fevers. Author notes difficulty of achieving this in West Africa context but presents it as essential to survival and lowering severity of attacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment/removal of subcutaneous/ocular filaria
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatment consists of getting the thing out, and the thing to be careful of is to get it out whole, for if any part of it is left in, suppuration sets in, so even if you are personally convinced you have got it out successfully it is just as well to wash out the wound with carbolic or Condy's fluid. The most frequent sufferers from these Filariae are the natives, but white people do get them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When removing filarial worms from skin or eye: extract the worm intact; if any part remains suppuration (infection) will occur. After removal irrigate/wash wound with antiseptic (carbolic acid or Condy's fluid). Be cautious and inspect for completeness of removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific procedure for Guinea-worm (Filaria medinensis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The native treatment of this pest is very cautiously to open the skin over the head of the worm and secure it between a little cleft bit of bamboo and then gradually wind the rest of the affair out. Only a small portion can be wound out at a time, as the wound is very liable to inflame, and should the worm break, it is certain to inflame badly, and a terrible wound will result. You cannot wind it out by the tail because you are then, so to speak, turning its fur the wrong way, and it catches in the wound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: open skin over the worm's head, secure head (e.g., with a small cleft bamboo), and slowly wind the worm out a little at a time over multiple sessions to avoid inflammation; never pull by the tail. Winding out is typically a morning task and can delay travel. Breakage of the worm causes severe inflammation and complications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical precaution about companions with Guinea-worm
rubrics_metrics.description: I should, I may remark, strongly advise any one who likes to start early on a canoe journey to see that no native member of the party has a Filaria medinensis on hand; for winding it up is always reserved for a morning job and as many other jobs are similarly reserved it makes for delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational advice: before departing on early journeys (e.g., canoe trips), ensure no companion needs Guinea-worm winding that morning, as the extraction is time-consuming and usually done in the morning, which can delay travel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectations about acclimatization and mortality
rubrics_metrics.description: Yet remember... that 85 per cent. of them die of fever or return home with their health permanently wrecked. Also remember that there is no getting acclimatised to the Coast. ... By far the largest class is the third, which is made up of those who have a slight dose of fever once a fortnight, and some day... get a heavy dose and die of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations: most newcomers will contract fever during a residence of more than six months; acclimatisation is not guaranteed. This is less an instruction than a caution to take all preventive measures seriously and to understand long-term risk categories (immune-like few, intermittent sufferers, cumulative poisoning, acute poisoning leading to early death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not be paralyzed by fear; take measured precaution
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the new-comer who goes to the Coast take the most cheerful view of these statements and let him regard himself as preordained to be one of the two most favoured classes. Let him take every care short of getting frightened, which is as deadly as taking no care at all...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological guidance: maintain morale and avoid excessive fear; take practical precautions conscientiously but avoid panic or fatalism, which the author claims is harmful to survival.
